title: Drawdown arithmetic and the protocol
teaches: A drawdown is how far the account is below its highest value, open trades included, checked at least weekly; every loss needs a bigger gain to repair (down 25% needs about 33%, down 50% needs 100%); our ladder cuts the max position as the drawdown deepens (normal cap 40%, then 10% at 6% down, 8% at 8%, 5% at 10%, no new trades at 15%), size comes back one rung each time half the drawdown is won back and the normal cap returns within 5% of the peak, and a monthly loss of 8% closes the month to new trades, with no daily or weekly limit.

facts.quote: A drawdown is typically quoted as the percentage difference between the peak of an investment and its following trough.
facts.claim: A drawdown is the percent drop from a peak to the low that follows it.

facts.quote: The drawdown would be calculated like this if an investment account of $20,000 dropped down to a value of $18,000 and then recovered to $20,000. The account experienced a 10% drawdown in this period:
facts.claim: An account that falls from $20,000 to $18,000 and then recovers has had a 10% drawdown.

facts.quote: This also demonstrates that a drawdown isn't always the same as a loss.
facts.claim: A drawdown is not always the same as your loss.

facts.quote: The XYZ stock experienced a drawdown of 27.3%, but the trader's unrealized loss at the $80 trough was $20 because they had purchased the stock at $100 per share, rather than the peak price of $110.
facts.claim: Drawdown runs from the peak ($110), while your loss runs from what you paid ($100), so the two differ.

facts.quote: If the price of XYZ stock then rises to a new peak of $120, drops to a new trough of $105, and then recovers to $120, that would be a new drawdown of $15 or 12.5%.
facts.claim: A stock bought at $100 that peaks at $120 and dips to $105 is in a 12.5% drawdown while still above cost.

facts.quote: The size of a drawdown is only one part of the measurement. Equally important is the time it takes to recover from a drawdown.
facts.claim: How long a drawdown takes to recover matters as much as how deep it is.

facts.quote: The primary risk associated with drawdowns is the uptick in share price needed to overcome that drawdown.
facts.claim: The main risk of a drawdown is the gain it takes to get back.

facts.quote: However, a fund that experiences a drawdown of 20% must recover significantly more of its share price to reach its peak again.
facts.claim: A 20% drawdown takes a much bigger climb to get back to the peak.

facts.quote: Maximum drawdown (MDD) is the largest decline in an investment's value from its peak to trough before a new peak is achieved.
facts.claim: Max drawdown is the biggest fall from a peak to a low before a new high.

facts.quote: The initial peak of $750,000 is used in the MDD calculation. The interim peak of $600,000 is not used, since it does not represent a new high.
facts.claim: A bounce that stays under the old high is not a new peak, so max drawdown still runs from the old high.

facts.quote: The MDD calculation takes into consideration the lowest portfolio value ($350,000 in this case) before a new peak is made, and not just the first drop to $400,000.
facts.claim: Max drawdown uses the lowest point before a new high, not just the first drop.

facts.quote: MDD only measures the largest loss size, not how often losses occur. MDD doesn't show how long recovery from the largest loss takes or if recovery happens.
facts.claim: Max drawdown shows how deep the worst fall was, not how long the recovery took or whether it came.

facts.quote: The largest cumulative percentage decline in the Net Asset Value of your portfolio from the highest or peak value to the lowest or trough value after the peak.
facts.claim: Max drawdown is the biggest percent fall in your account's value from its high to the low after it.

facts.quote: Ulcer Index measures the depth and duration of percentage drawdowns in price from earlier highs. The greater a drawdown in value, and the longer it takes to recover to earlier highs, the higher the UI.
facts.claim: Drawdowns run from earlier highs, and both their depth and the time to recover count.

facts.quote: For example a 50% loss requires a subsequent 100% gain to break-even. A given percentage loss always requires a greater percentage gain to break-even.
facts.claim: A 50% loss needs a 100% gain to get back to even, and every loss needs a bigger percent gain than itself.

facts.quote: Instead, many non-expert investors may assume for example that a 50% gain is sufficient to offset a 50% loss.
facts.claim: Many investors wrongly think a 50% gain makes up for a 50% loss.

facts.quote: While returns of +10% and –10% result in a total return of –1%, a return sequence of +50% and –50% results in a total return of –25%.
facts.claim: Up 10% then down 10% loses 1% overall; up 50% then down 50% loses 25%.

facts.quote: For returns of +/-50% a stock worth $100 increases to $150, before falling to $75.
facts.claim: Up 50% then down 50% turns $100 into $150, then $75.

facts.quote: The second percentage change multiplies both the initial value and the first percentage change.
facts.claim: Percent changes compound: each one applies to the value the last one left.

facts.quote: An unusual feature of percentage returns is that a subsequent 29.2% increase is required to reverse Black Monday's 22.6% decrease.
facts.claim: Black Monday's 22.6% drop needed a 29.2% gain to reverse.

facts.quote: For instance, to recover from a 10% loss, an investor needs an 11% gain. To recover from a 50% loss, an investor needs a 100% gain.
facts.claim: Down 10% needs about 11% back; down 50% needs 100% back.

facts.quote: The first contemporary global financial crisis unfolded on October 19, 1987, a day known as "Black Monday," when the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 22.6 percent.
facts.claim: On Black Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow fell 22.6% in one day.

facts.quote: the S&P 500 index fell 57 percent from its October 2007 peak to its trough in March 2009.
facts.claim: The S&P 500 fell 57% from its October 2007 peak to its March 2009 low.

facts.quote: Reduce position size. Less money at risk equals less pressure and clearer thinking. Traders can then increase position size as they demonstrate a new track record of executing their system.
facts.claim: After a big loss, trade smaller, then size back up as you prove you are following your system again.

facts.quote: Regardless of how a trader processes a blowup, it's best to get back into the market gradually by employing one of the following tactics:
facts.claim: After a big loss, come back to the market gradually.

facts.quote: The combination of a heightened emotional state and shallow thinking can lead to typical bad behaviors, such as ignoring stops, selling winners too soon, and doubling down after a loss.
facts.claim: Doubling down after a loss is one of the typical bad behaviors after a big hit.

facts.quote: They can also implement "circuit breakers" to prevent additional trading after a certain level of loss in a day.
facts.claim: Some traders set a loss level that stops further trading for the day.

facts.quote: For example, they could pledge to step away for the day if they lose a certain amount of money or take 15 minutes if they feel an urge to break a trading rule.
facts.claim: Commit in advance to step away for the day after losing a set amount.

facts.quote: As a trader works to figure out what needs fixing, there's no harm in reducing the size of your trades. Once your results get back on track, you can increase your risk-taking.
facts.claim: In a losing streak, trade smaller while you find the problem, and size back up once results recover.

facts.quote: Losing streaks can happen to the best of us, but sometimes a bout of bad luck can actually reflect a problem with our trading strategy.
facts.claim: A losing streak can be bad luck, or a sign that something in the strategy is broken.

facts.quote: The anti-Martingale system allows forex and other traders to increase their position size after profitable trades and reduce it after losses. This approach aims to maximize profit while limiting exposure during downturns.
facts.claim: Cutting size after losses and adding it back after wins is meant to limit your exposure in a downturn.

facts.quote: When a gambler who uses this method experiences a loss, they immediately double the size of the next bet.
facts.claim: The martingale method doubles the bet after every loss.

facts.quote: This assumes that the gambler has an unlimited supply of money to bet or at least enough to make it to the winning payoff.
facts.claim: Doubling after every loss only works if you have unlimited money, or enough to last until the win.

facts.quote: If that isn't the case, just a few successive losses under this system could lead to losing everything you came with.
facts.claim: Without unlimited money, doubling after losses can wipe you out in a few losses in a row.

facts.quote: The issue is that there is no way to predict when that will happen, before or after you run out of money.
facts.claim: You can't know when a losing run will turn, so betting that it must turn soon can run you out of money first.

facts.quote: To recoup their capital, or to seek “revenge” on the market after a string of losing trades, they may try to make up profits wherever they can, usually by increasing the size and frequency of their trades.
facts.claim: After a string of losses, traders often try to win it back by trading bigger and more often.

facts.quote: While this practice often results in poor performance
facts.claim: That kind of revenge trading often leads to poor results.

facts.quote: Managing risk on individual trades will also reduce the likelihood of a large drawdown, in turn reducing the psychological pitfalls that come from such circumstances.
facts.claim: Controlling the risk on each trade makes a large drawdown less likely.

facts.quote: Other traders use a drawdown concept to set a daily loss limit. They establish a target maximum allowable loss, and if they reach that target during the day, they end their activities at that point.
facts.claim: Some traders set a daily loss limit and stop trading for the day when they hit it.

facts.quote: How you set your drawdown limit is not relevant here, but once you do have it, you should have the discipline to observe it.
facts.claim: Whatever loss limit you set, obey it once it's hit.

facts.quote: To determine the correct position size from this information, the investor simply needs to divide the account risk ($500) by the trade risk ($20). This means 25 shares can be bought ($500 / $20).
facts.claim: Size comes from the stop: the dollars you will risk divided by the risk per share.

facts.quote: I lowered my max sizing to 5% down from 10% which is down from 20%.
facts.claim: As my drawdown deepened, I cut my max position size from 20% to 10% to 5%.

facts.quote: After a 6% drawdown I immediately reduce to 10% max. After an 8% drawdown I reduce to 8% max. And after 10% drawdown I reduce to 5% max.
facts.claim: Our ladder: after a 6% drawdown the max position is 10%; after 8%, 8%; after 10%, 5%.

facts.quote: A drawdown is how far the account is below its highest value, open trades included, checked at least weekly.
facts.claim: Our definition: a drawdown is how far the account sits below its highest value, open trades counted, checked at least weekly.

facts.quote: On the way down: under 6% down, the normal cap (A7); 6% down, max position 10%; 8% down, 8%; 10% down, 5%; 15% down, no new trades (B13).
facts.claim: Our ladder down: under 6% the normal cap; at 6% down a 10% max position; at 8%, 8%; at 10%, 5%; at 15%, no new trades.

facts.quote: At a 15% drawdown, stop opening new trades and review before trading again.
facts.claim: At a 15% drawdown we stop opening new trades and review before trading again.

facts.quote: Size comes back one rung of the ladder each time the account recovers half of the drawdown; full size again once the account is back within 5% of its peak.
facts.claim: The way back: one rung up each time the account wins back half of the drawdown, and the normal cap once the account is within 5% of its peak.

facts.quote: A7. Max position 40% of the account (raised from 20-25% on 2026-11-09: "RAISE THE CAP TO 40% ACTUALLY. ESPECIALLY WITH EARLY TRIMS AT 3-5R THAT IS FINE.").
facts.claim: Our normal cap is 40% of the account, raised on 2026-11-09 from the old 20% to 25%.

facts.quote: B15. No daily loss limit. ("15, no.")
facts.claim: We have no daily loss limit.

facts.quote: No weekly loss limit; a monthly loss limit of 8%: at 8% down in a calendar month (from the month's starting value), no new trades for the rest of the month.
facts.claim: No weekly loss limit; at 8% down from the month's starting value, no new trades for the rest of the calendar month.

facts.quote: No losing-streak rule: size is cut only by the drawdown ladder, in percent (A8, B13, B14).
facts.claim: We have no losing-streak rule; only the drawdown ladder, in percent, cuts size.

facts.quote: A tight stop never justifies a bigger position than that: a gap can jump the stop.
facts.claim: A tight stop never earns a position above the cap, because a gap can jump the stop.

facts.quote: A stop order becomes a market order once the stop price is reached. The price you receive upon execution, though, could be markedly different than your stop price.
facts.claim: Once triggered, a stop is a market order and can fill far from the stop price.

walkthroughs.title: Measured from the high
steps: A drawdown is the drop from your account's high to the low that follows, as a percent of the high.
Investopedia's example: an account at $20,000 drops to $18,000, then recovers. That's a 10% drawdown.
It runs from the peak, not from what you paid. So it isn't always the same as your loss.

walkthroughs.title: Losses cost more to fix
steps: Down 10%, you need about an 11% gain to get back. Down 50%, you need 100%.
The gain is earned on what's left, so it always has to be bigger than the loss.
Up 50% then down 50% is not even. $100 goes to $150, then to $75.

walkthroughs.title: Our drawdown ladder, down and back up
steps: A drawdown is how far the account sits below its highest value, open trades included. We check it at least weekly.
Under 6% down, the normal cap of 40%. At 6% down, a 10% max position. At 8%, 8%. At 10%, 5%.
At 15% down, no new trades. Review before you trade again.
Back up: one rung each time you win back half the drawdown. The normal cap returns within 5% of the peak.

questions.q: What does a drawdown measure?
choices: The drop from a high to the low after it
Your loss from the price you paid
The average size of your losses
questions.answer: The drop from a high to the low after it
questions.why: The drop from a high to the low after it. A drawdown is the percent fall from a peak to the trough that follows.
questions.lesson_line: A drawdown starts at the high, not at your cost.

wrong.Your loss from the price you paid: That's your loss on the trade. Drawdown runs from the peak, and the two are not always the same.
wrong.The average size of your losses: That's your typical loss per trade. A drawdown is the whole fall from a high, and it can span many trades.
wrong.Your worst single-day loss: A drawdown can build over many days. It runs from the high to the lowest point after it.

questions.q: Your drawdown is measured from your account's highest value, not from what you started with.
questions.why: True. Drawdown runs from the peak. In Investopedia's example, a stock bought at $100 that peaks at $120 and dips to $105 is in a 12.5% drawdown while still above cost.
questions.lesson_line: You can be up on the year and still be in a drawdown.

questions.q: Fill in the gain.
questions.sentence: A 50% loss needs a ___ gain to get back to even.
questions.why: 100%. Half the account is gone, so what's left has to double. Many investors wrongly assume a 50% gain is enough.
questions.lesson_line: Down 50% means you have to double just to get back to even.

questions.q: Your account peaked at $50,000. It's now $42,500. What's your drawdown?
questions.why: 15%. Take the drop from $50,000 to $42,500 and divide it by the peak, $50,000.
questions.lesson_line: Drawdown is the peak minus the low, divided by the peak.

questions.q: A 10% loss needs about an 11% gain to get back to even.
questions.why: True. Small losses are cheap to fix: down 10% needs an 11% gain. Down 50% needs a 100% gain.
questions.lesson_line: Keep losses small. They're cheap to fix while they're small.

questions.q: You're down 25% from your account's high. Roughly what gain gets you back to the high?
questions.why: About 33%. The gain is earned on the smaller account, so a 25% loss takes more than 25% to win back.
questions.lesson_line: Down 25% needs about 33% back. Every loss costs more to fix than it cost to take.

wrong.25%: That's the trap. A 25% gain on the smaller account leaves you short of the high.
wrong.About 20%: Backwards. A 20% loss is what wipes out a 25% gain. Fixing a 25% loss takes more, not less.

questions.q: A 50% gain followed by a 50% loss leaves you back where you started.
questions.why: False. Up 50% takes $100 to $150. Down 50% takes $150 to $75. You end up down 25%.
questions.lesson_line: Equal percent gains and losses don't cancel out. You end up behind.

questions.q: On our drawdown ladder, what's your max position size after a 6% drawdown?
questions.why: 10% of the account. After a 6% drawdown, our max position drops to 10%. Deeper drawdowns cut it again.
questions.lesson_line: The deeper the drawdown, the smaller the max position.

wrong.20% of the account: That was our old normal max. Today the cap is 40%, and either way the 6% step cuts it to 10%.
wrong.5% of the account: That's the cap after a 10% drawdown. At 6%, the cap is 10%.
wrong.6% of the account: That mixes up the drawdown and the size. A 6% drawdown sets a 10% max.

questions.q: You started the year at $40,000, ran it to $50,000, and now sit at $45,000. What's your drawdown?
questions.why: 10%. Drawdown runs from the peak, $50,000, not from where you started. You're up on the year and in a 10% drawdown at the same time.
questions.lesson_line: Measure from the high, not from where you began.

questions.q: Your account fell from $50,000 to $40,000. What percent gain takes it back to $50,000?
questions.why: 25%. The gain has to be earned on $40,000, not $50,000. That 20% drop needs a 25% climb.
questions.lesson_line: Gains are earned on what's left. That's why every loss costs more to fix.

questions.q: Two accounts each had a 20% max drawdown. So both took the same time to recover.
questions.why: False. Max drawdown shows how deep the worst fall was, not how long the climb back took, or whether it came. Depth and time are two separate measures.
questions.lesson_line: Ask two things about any drawdown: how deep, and how long.

questions.story: Your account runs from $100,000 to $120,000, drops to $96,000, bounces to $110,000, then sinks to $90,000. Later it makes a new high at $130,000.
questions.q: What was the max drawdown?
questions.why: 25%. The high was $120,000 and the lowest point before a new high was $90,000. The bounce to $110,000 never made a new high, so it doesn't reset the peak.
questions.lesson_line: Max drawdown runs from the high to the lowest low before a new high.

wrong.About 18%: That measures from the $110,000 bounce. A bounce that stays under the old high is not a new peak.
wrong.20%: That's only the first drop, $120,000 to $96,000. The low that counts is the lowest one before a new high.
wrong.10%: That measures from your start, $100,000. Drawdown runs from the peak.

questions.story: Your account sits at its high. Each trade risks 2% of the account as it stands. A cold spell hands you ten full losers in a row.
questions.q: How deep is your drawdown now?
questions.why: About 18%. Each 2% loss comes off a smaller account, so ten of them land a bit under 20%. That's a deep hole from losses that each looked normal.
questions.lesson_line: Your risk per trade sets how deep a cold streak can dig.

wrong.20%: That's ten losses of 2% of the starting account. Here each 2% comes off a smaller account, so the total is a bit less.
wrong.2%: That's one loss. Ten in a row stack up.

questions.story: You're 7% below your account's high. An A+ setup shows up, one you really like.
questions.q: Under our drawdown ladder, what's the most you put in it?
questions.why: 10% of the account. A 7% drawdown is past the 6% step, so your max is 10%. The 8% step hasn't kicked in yet.
questions.lesson_line: The ladder reads your drawdown, not how much you like the setup.

wrong.20% of the account: That was our old normal max. Today the cap is 40%, and the 6% step already cut it to 10%.
wrong.8% of the account: That cap starts at an 8% drawdown. You're at 7%, so the most is still 10%.
wrong.5% of the account: That's the cap after a 10% drawdown. You can go smaller, but the most here is 10%.

questions.q: Your account is $90,000, down 10% from its high. Under our drawdown ladder, what's the most you put in one stock?
questions.why: $4,500. After a 10% drawdown, our max position is 5% of the account, and 5% of $90,000 is $4,500.
questions.lesson_line: Find your step on the ladder first. Then turn the percent into dollars.

questions.q: Doubling your size after every loss can wipe out an account in just a few losses in a row.
questions.why: True. That's the martingale method. It needs bottomless money, and without it a few straight losses can take everything. Schwab lists doubling down after a loss as a typical bad behavior.
questions.lesson_line: Never double up to win a loss back. That's how a drawdown turns into a blowup.

questions.story: Before the open, you set a loss limit for the day. By midday your losses hit it. A setup you like starts to form.
questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Take it with a tighter stop
Raise the limit and take it
questions.why: Stop trading for the day. Traders who use a daily loss limit end their trading when they reach it. A limit only works if you obey it.
questions.lesson_line: Set the limit when you're calm. Obey it when you're not.

wrong.Take it with a tighter stop: You're still trading past your limit. A tighter stop doesn't change that you're done for the day.
wrong.Take it at double size: That's trying to win the day back. Doubling down after a loss is how a bad day becomes a big drawdown.
wrong.Raise the limit and take it: A limit you move once it's hit isn't a limit. Once you have it, have the discipline to obey it.

questions.q: On Black Monday, October 19, 1987, the Dow fell 22.6% in one day. What gain did it need to win that back? Use one decimal.
questions.why: 29.2%. One session took 22.6%, and reversing it took a 29.2% gain. The climb back is always bigger than the fall.
questions.lesson_line: Every drop needs a bigger gain to undo it. Even a single day's.

questions.q: The S&P 500 fell 57% from its October 2007 peak to its March 2009 low. Roughly what gain did it need to get back?
questions.why: About 133%. After a 57% fall the index had to more than double just to get back to its peak. Deep drawdowns are brutal to repair.
questions.lesson_line: Past 50% down, you need more than a double just to get back to even.

wrong.57%: That's the equal-percent trap. A 57% gain on what was left falls far short of the old peak.
wrong.About 100%: 100% fixes a 50% loss. This fall was deeper, so the climb back was steeper.

questions.story: A cold month leaves you 8% below your account's high. Your last six trades were all losers.
questions.q: What's your next move?
choices: Trade smaller and find what's wrong
Trade more often to make it back
Press on, a win is due
questions.answer: Trade smaller and find what's wrong
questions.why: Trade smaller and find what's wrong. A streak can be bad luck or a broken strategy, so cut size while you check. Our ladder already caps a position at 8% of the account here.
questions.lesson_line: In a drawdown, shrink first and diagnose second.

wrong.Trade more often to make it back: That's revenge trading. Trading bigger and more often to win it back often ends in poor results.
wrong.Press on, a win is due: No win is ever due. There's no way to know when a streak ends, and betting that it must can run you out of money first.

questions.q: Ten 2% losses in a row, each 2% of what's left, leave you about 18.3% below your high. To the nearest percent, what gain gets you back?
questions.why: 22%. The 18.3% hole has to be climbed from a smaller base, so it takes more than 18.3% to fix. That's what one cold streak at 2% a trade costs.
questions.lesson_line: Ten 2% losses dig an 18.3% hole that takes 22% to climb out of.

questions.story: A rough stretch put you deep in a drawdown, so you cut your size. Your last five trades followed your plan and worked.
questions.q: How do you bring your size back?
choices: A step at a time, as it keeps working
All at once, the slump is over
Bigger than before, to catch up
questions.answer: A step at a time, as it keeps working
questions.why: A step at a time, as it keeps working. Size comes back as you build a new track record of following your system, not in one jump.
questions.lesson_line: Cut size fast in a drawdown. Add it back slowly.

wrong.All at once, the slump is over: One good run doesn't rebuild the record. Coming back gradually is the safer path after a big hit.
wrong.Bigger than before, to catch up: That's sizing up to make the drawdown back. Trading bigger to win it back often ends in poor results.

questions.story: You're 8% below your account's high. You risk 1% a trade. Your best setup in months has an honest stop 5% below entry.
questions.q: Under our drawdown ladder, how big is the position?
questions.why: 8% of the account. Your 1% risk over a 5% stop says 20%, but after an 8% drawdown our max is 8%. The cap wins, and you end up risking less than 1%.
questions.lesson_line: Size from the stop, then apply the ladder. The smaller number wins.

wrong.20% of the account: That's 1% risk over a 5% stop with no cap. In an 8% drawdown, the max is 8%.
wrong.1% of the account: 1% is your risk, not your position. They're two different numbers.
wrong.10% of the account: 10% is the cap from the 6% step. At an 8% drawdown the cap is 8%.

questions.q: Under our rule, a drawdown counts only closed trades; open positions don't move it.
questions.why: False. A drawdown is how far the account is below its highest value, open trades included. An open loser is part of the hole, whether or not you've sold it.
questions.lesson_line: Drawdown is measured on the whole account, open trades included.

questions.q: How often, at least, do we check the account's drawdown?
questions.why: At least weekly. The ladder reads the drawdown, so the drawdown has to be read on a schedule. Weekly is the minimum; more often is fine.
questions.lesson_line: Check the drawdown at least weekly. The ladder can only work on a number you've looked at.

wrong.Only at month end: Too slow. A 6% step can arrive and pass inside a month. Weekly at least.
wrong.After every trade: You can, but the rule asks for weekly at least. A schedule beats a reaction.
wrong.Only after a losing streak: We have no losing-streak rule. The ladder runs on the drawdown percent, checked weekly whatever the streak.

questions.q: Fill in our rule.
questions.sentence: At a ___ drawdown we stop opening new trades and review.
questions.why: 15%. At 10% down the max position is 5%. At 15% down, no new trades at all, and a review before trading again.
questions.lesson_line: At 15% down the ladder ends in a stop: no new trades, review first.

questions.q: Our rules include a daily loss limit: lose a set amount in a day and you're done for the day.
questions.why: False. We have no daily and no weekly loss limit. Our limits are the drawdown ladder, read from the account's high, and a monthly loss limit of 8% from the month's starting value.
questions.lesson_line: No daily or weekly limit. The ladder and the 8% monthly limit do the job.

questions.q: You started the month at $60,000. At what account value does our monthly loss limit stop new trades for the month?
questions.why: $55,200. That's 8% below the month's starting value of $60,000. From there, no new trades until the calendar month ends. Once you have a limit, obey it.
questions.lesson_line: Monthly limit: 8% down from where the month started, and the month is closed to new trades.

questions.story: Your account peaked at $100,000 and sank to $88,000, a 12% drawdown, so your max position fell to 5%. It has climbed back to $94,000.
questions.q: Under our ladder, what's your max position now?
questions.why: 8% of the account. At $94,000 you've won back half of the fall from $100,000 to $88,000. Half back earns one rung up, from the 5% rung to the 8% rung.
questions.lesson_line: The way back is one rung at a time: half the drawdown won back, one rung up.

wrong.5% of the account: That was the cap at the low. Winning back half of the drawdown earns one rung back.
wrong.10% of the account: That's two rungs up. Half of the drawdown won back earns one rung, not two.
wrong.40% of the account: The normal cap returns once the account is within 5% of its peak. At $94,000 you're still more than 5% below $100,000.

questions.q: Your account peaked at $80,000 and fell 10%. Under our rule, at what value does the normal cap come back?
questions.why: $76,000. The normal cap returns once the account is back within 5% of its peak, and 5% under $80,000 is $76,000. Until then you climb the rungs: 5%, then 8%, then 10%.
questions.lesson_line: Full size again within 5% of the peak. Not at the peak, not at the first green week.

questions.story: Your account sits at its high. You risk 1% a trade. A setup you love has a tight stop 1% under entry, so the risk math says a 100% position.
questions.q: Under our rules, what's the most you can put in it?
questions.why: 40% of the account. That's our normal cap, and a tight stop never justifies more. A triggered stop is a market order, and a gap can fill you far past it.
questions.lesson_line: The cap is 40%. A tight stop shrinks the risk math, never the cap.

wrong.100% of the account: That's the risk math with no cap. A 1% stop can be gapped through, and 100% of the account in one stock is how a gap ruins a year.
wrong.20% of the account: That was our old normal max. The cap is 40% now.
wrong.10% of the account: That's the cap after a 6% drawdown. At the high, the normal cap applies.

questions.story: A brutal quarter. Your account is 15% below its high, open positions included. A clean setup triggers today.
questions.q: What does our rule say?
choices: Take it at half your usual risk
Take it, the ladder only caps size
questions.why: No new trades, review first. At 15% down the ladder stops opening trades. A streak can be bad luck or a broken strategy; the review is where you find out which.
questions.lesson_line: At 15% down, the answer to any setup is no. Review, then earn the way back.

wrong.Take it at 5% max: 5% is the rung for 10% down. At 15% the ladder stops new trades altogether.
wrong.Take it at half your usual risk: Smaller risk is still a new trade. At 15% down there are none until you've reviewed.
wrong.Take it, the ladder only caps size: The ladder caps size down to 10% down. At 15% it stops you.

questions.story: Your account peaked at $100,000 in the summer. It started this month at $95,000 and sits at $87,000 today, 13% below the peak.
questions.q: What stops you from opening new trades today?
choices: Nothing, the ladder just caps size
questions.why: The monthly loss limit. From $95,000 to $87,000 is more than 8% down this month, so no new trades until the month ends. The 13% drawdown caps a position at 5% but doesn't stop you.
questions.lesson_line: Two clocks run at once: the ladder from the peak, the 8% limit from the month's start. Either can stop you.

wrong.The 15% drawdown stop: You're 13% below the peak, short of the 15% stop. Here the ladder caps size at 5%; it's the month that stops you.
wrong.Nothing, the ladder just caps size: The ladder alone would let you trade at a 5% max. But the month's loss has passed 8%, and that closes the month.
wrong.The daily loss limit: We have no daily loss limit. The monthly limit is the one that bites here.
